name: How to Say No
title: How to Say No
answer: This idea is about agreeing on clear exit criteria before a pilot begins, so a school can stop using a tool without a difficult argument if it fails. It matters because it protects teachers, students, and the budget from tools that seem appealing but do not work, and it makes honest endings as normal as scaling up.

sections.body: A school can find it hard to say no to an AI tool once teachers like it and the vendor is friendly. The idea is to decide in advance what would cause the pilot to stop, so the decision is already made if those conditions occur. This removes the need to start a fresh debate when results are disappointing or a problem appears. Specific exit criteria protect teachers, students, and the budget from tools that feel good but do not work. The text presents this as part of a pilot, measure, scale discipline.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: Before a pilot starts, the school agrees on specific exit criteria. The tool should stop if the main measure does not improve against the baseline or the comparison group. It should also stop if a serious privacy or safety incident occurs, or if the vendor will not sign the agreement the district needs to scale. Another stop condition is when the tool works only for some students and leaves others, such as students with disabilities or English learners, further behind. The text does not give grade bands, so the same logic applies across a school or district pilot, and when a pilot stops the school reports it as openly as scaling with a short note to staff about what was tested, the results, and why it stopped.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or finding for this idea beyond the statement that Figure 4.7 lists the exit criteria. It does not offer an evidence label or research result. This idea therefore rests on practice rather than research, as the book presents it.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main limit is that saying no is hard once teachers like a tool and the vendor is friendly, so the exit criteria must be agreed before the pilot starts. The criteria need to be specific, otherwise the school may still argue from scratch. The text names the risks to watch: no improvement on the main measure, a serious privacy or safety incident, a vendor that will not sign the agreement needed to scale, and a tool that helps only some students while leaving others further behind. The decision to stop is made by the pre-agreed criteria rather than by a person improvising under pressure, though people still set those criteria and report the outcome. Stopping should be reported as openly as scaling, because honest endings build trust and make teachers more willing to volunteer for the next pilot.
